author: William Blake
poem_text_en:
I was angry with my friend;
I told my wrath, my wrath did end.
I was angry with my foe:
I told it not, my wrath did grow.

And I water’d it in fears,
Night and morning with my tears:
And I sunned it with smiles,
And with soft deceitful wiles.

And it grew both day and night,
Till it bore an apple bright.
And my foe beheld it shine,
And he knew that it was mine.

And into my garden stole,
When the night had veiled the pole;
In the morning glad I see,
My foe outstretched beneath the tree.
summary_en: The poem illustrates how suppressed anger grows and turns into a deadly force, whereas expressed anger dissipates. The speaker nourishes their wrath against an enemy until it manifests as a poisonous tree with a deceptive fruit. Ultimately, this hatred leads to the physical downfall of the enemy.

figures_of_speech.example_en: And I sunned it with smiles
figures_of_speech.note_en: The sound /s/ is repeated in 'sunned' and 'smiles'.
The anger is compared to a growing tree.

rules.rule_en: The poet of A Poison Tree is William Blake (1757–1827), an English poet, painter, and printmaker.
The rhyme scheme of the poem is AABB (rhyming couplets).
Suppressed anger is metaphorically represented as a growing tree watered by tears and fears.
